claim: 23,126 phosphosites were quantified in skeletal muscle across five genetically distinct mouse strains in two dietary environments with and without acute in vivo insulin stimulation.
source: Using mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics, we quantified 23,126 phosphosites in skeletal muscle of five genetically distinct mouse strains in two dietary environments, with and without acute in vivo insulin stimulation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of phosphosites quantified and the experimental conditions.

claim: Almost half of the insulin-regulated phosphoproteome was modified by genetic background on an ordinary diet.
source: Almost half of the insulin-regulated phosphoproteome was modified by genetic background on an ordinary diet, and high-fat high-sugar feeding affected insulin signalling in a strain-dependent manner.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the phosphoproteomics data analysis.

claim: High-fat high-sugar feeding affected insulin signalling in a strain-dependent manner.
source: Almost half of the insulin-regulated phosphoproteome was modified by genetic background on an ordinary diet, and high-fat high-sugar feeding affected insulin signalling in a strain-dependent manner.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the phosphoproteomics data analysis.

claim: The data revealed coregulated subnetworks within the insulin signalling pathway.
source: Our data revealed coregulated subnetworks within the insulin signalling pathway, expanding our understanding of the pathway's organisation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: S469 on Pfkfb2 is a regulatory phosphosite and a key activator of glycolysis.
source: Furthermore, associating diverse signalling responses with insulin-stimulated glucose uptake uncovered regulators of muscle insulin responsiveness, including the regulatory phosphosite S469 on Pfkfb2, a key activator of glycolysis.
evidence: The abstract identifies S469 on Pfkfb2 as a regulator of insulin responsiveness based on correlation analysis.

claim: Glycolysis modulates insulin action in insulin resistance.
source: Finally, we confirmed the role of glycolysis in modulating insulin action in insulin resistance.
evidence: The abstract states this was confirmed through experimental validation.

claim: Genetics shapes global signalling responses and their adaptability to environmental changes.
source: Our results underscore the significance of genetics in shaping global signalling responses and their adaptability to environmental changes, emphasising the utility of studying biological diversity with phosphoproteomics to discover key regulatory mechanisms of complex traits.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the overall findings of the study.

claim: Protein phosphorylation enables cells to rapidly respond to environmental changes by modifying protein function at low metabolic cost.
source: Protein post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation enable cells to rapidly respond to environmental changes by modifying protein function at low metabolic cost (Humphrey et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation is involved in nearly all biological processes and is dysregulated in numerous complex diseases.
source: As a result of this high metabolic efficiency, phosphorylation is involved in nearly all biological processes and is dysregulated in numerous complex diseases (Needham et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: More than 100,000 phosphosites have been discovered through advances in mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics.
source: Advances in mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics – the unbiased identification and quantification of protein phosphorylation – have led to the discovery of more than 100,000 phosphosites, revealing that the phosphoproteome comprises vast, interconnected phosphorylation networks (Olsen et al., 2006; Bodenmiller et al., 2010; Needham et al., 2019a; Leutert et al., 2023), rather than the textbook view of isolated, linear kinase cascades.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The phosphoproteome comprises vast, interconnected phosphorylation networks rather than isolated, linear kinase cascades.
source: Advances in mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics – the unbiased identification and quantification of protein phosphorylation – have led to the discovery of more than 100,000 phosphosites, revealing that the phosphoproteome comprises vast, interconnected phosphorylation networks (Olsen et al., 2006; Bodenmiller et al., 2010; Needham et al., 2019a; Leutert et al., 2023), rather than the textbook view of isolated, linear kinase cascades.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Post-prandial increases in blood glucose stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion.
source: Post-prandial increases in blood glucose stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion, coordinating a metabolic switch in target tissues like skeletal muscle and adipose (Haeusler et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Insulin increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue by promoting translocation of the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the plasma membrane.
source: Insulin increases glucose uptake into these tissues by promoting translocation of the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the plasma membrane, and serves other functions like enhancing protein synthesis, downregulating lipid catabolism, and altering gene transcription (Haeusler et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Insulin triggers a phosphorylation cascade primarily involving activation of the Ser/Thr kinase Akt.
source: To coordinate these functions, insulin triggers a phosphorylation cascade primarily involving activation of the Ser/Thr kinase Akt, regulation of downstream kinases including mTORC1 and GSK3, and modulation of parallel signalling arms (Haeusler et al., 2018; Gehart et al., 2010; Sylow et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The insulin signalling cascade regulates over a thousand phosphosites.
source: Seminal phosphoproteomics studies demonstrated that this cascade regulates over a thousand phosphosites, with many still uncharacterised in insulin action (Humphrey et al., 2013; Humphrey et al., 2015a; Krüger et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior phosphoproteomics studies.

claim: Insulin resistance is triggered by genetic and environmental factors such as family history of metabolic disease and high-calorie diets.
source: Insulin resistance – the failure of insulin to promote glucose uptake in its target tissues – is triggered by genetic and environmental factors such as family history of metabolic disease and high-calorie diets (James et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanistic basis of insulin resistance remains unresolved.
source: Although insulin resistance is a major precursor of metabolic disease including type 2 diabetes, its mechanistic basis remains unresolved (James et al., 2021; Fazakerley et al., 2019; van Gerwen et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interactions between genetics and environment significantly regulate biomolecular processes, including insulin resistance.
source: Interactions between genetics and environment significantly regulate biomolecular processes, including insulin resistance (Civelek and Lusis, 2014; Hunter, 2005; Nelson et al., 2022; Montgomery et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signalling pathways are likely a major conduit of gene-by-environment interactions.
source: As signalling pathways connect the extracellular environment to intracellular proteins, they are likely a major conduit of gene-by-environment interactions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the role of signalling pathways.

claim: How global phosphorylation signalling networks are regulated across different genetic backgrounds is relatively unexplored.
source: Yet, how global phosphorylation signalling networks are regulated across different genetic backgrounds is relatively unexplored.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Recent phosphoproteomics studies in yeast and mice identified genetic variants affecting multiple phosphosites.
source: Recent phosphoproteomics studies in yeast (Grossbach et al., 2022) and mice (Zhang et al., 2023) identified genetic variants affecting multiple phosphosites, but did not analyse the phosphoproteome's response to acute perturbation, which is crucial to its role as a signal transduction system.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Marked variation in acute signalling responses to exercise or insulin exists across individuals.
source: We have also shown marked variation in acute signalling responses to exercise or insulin across individuals (Needham et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: 28,809 phosphopeptides were quantified across 95 biological samples.
source: Using the EasyPhos workflow and data-independent acquisition (DIA) mass spectrometry (Humphrey et al., 2018; Bekker-Jensen et al., 2020), we quantified 28,809 phosphopeptides across 95 biological samples, corresponding to 23,126 unique high-confidence phosphosites (class I; localisation score >0.75) on 3507 proteins (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: On average, 15,395 phosphopeptides were quantified in each sample.
source: On average, we quantified 15,395 phosphopeptides in each sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: 441 insulin-regulated phosphopeptides on 232 proteins were identified.
source: This resulted in 441 insulin-regulated phosphopeptides on 232 proteins, which is noticeably more than recent studies of 10 min insulin signalling in patient-derived myoblasts (174 phosphopeptides; Batista et al., 2020) and 242 phosphopeptides (Haider et al., 2021) or mouse adipose tissue (319 phosphopeptides; Fazakerley et al., 2023; Figure 1b and c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results with comparison to prior studies.

claim: The analysis recovered many well-studied insulin-regulated phosphosites, including Akt substrates such as T247 on Akt1s1 (PRAS40), S939 on Tsc2, and S9 on Gsk3β.
source: Our analysis recovered many well-studied insulin-regulated phosphosites, including Akt substrates such as T247 on Akt1s1 (PRAS40), S939 on Tsc2, and S9 on Gsk3β (Figure 1d–f), as well as targets of downstream kinases including the Gsk3β substrate S641 on Gys1 (Figure 1g).
evidence: This statement is supported by the data and references to figures showing these phosphosites.

claim: Insulin-regulated phosphosites were enriched for insulin regulation in a previous human skeletal muscle phosphoproteome study.
source: Furthermore, insulin-regulated phosphosites were enriched for insulin regulation in our previous human skeletal muscle phosphoproteome (fold enrichment = 4.22, p=9.50 × 10–24, one-sided Fisher's exact test, Figure 1—figure supplement 3b; Needham et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis comparing to a prior study.

claim: Only half of all insulin-regulated phosphopeptides (228/441) were previously annotated as insulin-regulated in the PhosphositePlus database.
source: Despite this, only half of all insulin-regulated phosphopeptides (228/441) were previously annotated as insulin-regulated in the PhosphositePlus database (Hornbeck et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 3c), highlighting the potential of our data to discover novel aspects of insulin signalling while recapitulating known components.
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison to an existing database.

claim: Almost half of the 441 insulin-regulated phosphopeptides displayed a Strain effect.
source: Almost half of the 441 insulin-regulated phosphopeptides displayed a Strain effect (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: Vamp3 S48 is predicted to be highly functional (functional score = 0.750).
source: Vamp3 S48 is predicted to be highly functional (functional score = 0.750) (Ochoa et al., 2020), its phosphorylation correlates with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated and/or exercised human skeletal muscle (Needham et al., 2022), and Vamp3 overexpression rescues GLUT4 translocation in insulin resistance (Schwenk et al., 2012), suggesting that this site may represent a genetically variable control point of GLUT4 trafficking.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vamp3 S48 phosphorylation correlates with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated and/or exercised human skeletal muscle.
source: Vamp3 S48 is predicted to be highly functional (functional score = 0.750) (Ochoa et al., 2020), its phosphorylation correlates with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated and/or exercised human skeletal muscle (Needham et al., 2022), and Vamp3 overexpression rescues GLUT4 translocation in insulin resistance (Schwenk et al., 2012), suggesting that this site may represent a genetically variable control point of GLUT4 trafficking.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Vamp3 overexpression rescues GLUT4 translocation in insulin resistance.
source: Vamp3 S48 is predicted to be highly functional (functional score = 0.750) (Ochoa et al., 2020), its phosphorylation correlates with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated and/or exercised human skeletal muscle (Needham et al., 2022), and Vamp3 overexpression rescues GLUT4 translocation in insulin resistance (Schwenk et al., 2012), suggesting that this site may represent a genetically variable control point of GLUT4 trafficking.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Insulin responses were weaker in the four remaining strains compared to C57Bl6J.
source: In general, insulin responses were weaker in the four remaining strains compared to C57Bl6J, though the extent of this trend was strain-dependent (Figure 2e).
evidence: This statement is supported by the data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Strain×Diet effects were more prevalent than Uniform diet effects (110 vs 10 phosphopeptides).
source: Strain×Diet effects were more prevalent than Uniform diet effects (110 vs 10 phosphopeptides, Figure 2g; Supplementary file 1), suggesting that the molecular impact of dietary perturbation was strongly modulated by genetic background.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: Map2k4 activates p38 and JNK kinases which have been implicated as drivers of HFD-induced insulin resistance.
source: Map2k4 activates p38 and JNK kinases which have been implicated as drivers of HFD-induced insulin resistance (Gehart et al., 2010), and based on the behaviour of S78, the orchestration of this detrimental signalling axis in HFD-feeding may depend on genetic background.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Strain and diet affected multiple highly studied signalling sites, including Tsc2 S939, Gsk3α S21, and Tbc1d4 T649.
source: Strain and diet affected multiple highly studied signalling sites, including Tsc2 S939 (Diet effect), Gsk3α S21 (Strain and Diet effects), and Tbc1d4 T649 (Strain and Diet effects), while other sites such as Gsk3β S9 and Akt1s1 T247 were unaffected.
evidence: This statement is supported by the analysis of the curated network.

claim: Gsk3β S9 and Akt1s1 T247 were unaffected by strain and diet.
source: Strain and diet affected multiple highly studied signalling sites, including Tsc2 S939 (Diet effect), Gsk3α S21 (Strain and Diet effects), and Tbc1d4 T649 (Strain and Diet effects), while other sites such as Gsk3β S9 and Akt1s1 T247 were unaffected.
evidence: This statement is supported by the analysis of the curated network.

claim: Strain and diet affected both canonical and non-canonical insulin signalling proteins to a similar extent.
source: Interestingly, strain and diet affected both canonical and non-canonical insulin signalling proteins to a similar extent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3h–i).
evidence: This statement is supported by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Strain and Diet effects overlapped significantly (fold enrichment = 1.50, p=4.40 × 10–9).
source: Interestingly, Strain and Diet effects overlapped significantly (fold enrichment = 1.50, p=4.40 × 10–9, two-sided Fisher's exact test, Figure 1—figure supplement 3j), implying some phosphosites may be more amenable to regulation overall.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: KSEA accurately captured the activation of canonical insulin-regulated kinases (Akt, mTOR, p70S6K, and p90RSK) and the deactivation of GSK3.
source: KSEA accurately captured the activation of canonical insulin-regulated kinases (Akt, mTOR, p70S6K, and p90RSK) and the deactivation of GSK3, confirming the validity of the approach (Figure 4a).
evidence: This statement is supported by the KSEA analysis results.

claim: Seven kinases were differentially enriched across mouse strains in CHOW-fed mice (ANOVA adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: Focussing on CHOW-fed mice, we identified seven kinases differentially enriched across mouse strains (ANOVA adjusted p-value <0.05, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the KSEA analysis results.

claim: Strain×Diet effects on kinases were more prevalent than Uniform diet effects (five kinases compared to one).
source: Extending this analysis to all mice, we identified kinases with Uniform diet or Strain×Diet effects (Figure 4c). Akin to our analysis of individual phosphosites (Figure 2), Strain×Diet effects were more prevalent than Uniform diet effects (five kinases compared to one), indicating that genetic background strongly influences the impact of HFD-feeding on kinase signalling.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the KSEA analysis results.

claim: Tsc2 S939 and Akt1s1 T247 insulin responses correlated poorly (r=0.202, p=0.168).
source: For instance, while Tsc2 S939 and Akt1s1 T247 both activate mTORC1, their insulin responses correlated poorly (r=0.202, p=0.168, Figure 5b).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed four distinct groups of positively correlated Akt substrates.
source: Hierarchical clustering revealed four distinct groups of positively correlated Akt substrates (Figure 5a), suggesting these groups may coordinate distinct functional outputs of Akt signalling.
evidence: This statement is supported by the clustering analysis.

claim: WGCNA identified eight subnetworks of coregulated insulin-responsive phosphopeptides varying in size from 16 to 120 phosphopeptides, with 91 assigned to no subnetwork.
source: By performing weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA; Zhang and Horvath, 2005; Langfelder and Horvath, 2008), we identified eight subnetworks of coregulated insulin-responsive phosphopeptides (Figure 5c) varying in size from 16 to 120 phosphopeptides, with 91 assigned to no subnetwork (Figure 5d, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the WGCNA analysis results.

claim: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake differed by more than twofold across strains (two-way ANOVA strain effect p=4.78 × 10–7).
source: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake differed by more than twofold across strains (two-way ANOVA strain effect p=4.78 × 10–7) and was almost uniformly decreased by HFD-feeding (two-way ANOVA diet effect p=1.83 × 10–5) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of glucose uptake measurements.

claim: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake was almost uniformly decreased by HFD-feeding (two-way ANOVA diet effect p=1.83 × 10–5).
source: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake differed by more than twofold across strains (two-way ANOVA strain effect p=4.78 × 10–7) and was almost uniformly decreased by HFD-feeding (two-way ANOVA diet effect p=1.83 × 10–5) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of glucose uptake measurements.

claim: 37 phosphopeptides significantly correlated with insulin-stimulated glucose uptake using insulin-stimulated phosphopeptide intensity (r>0.35 or <–0.35, q-value <0.1).
source: To prioritise signalling nodes responsible for differences in insulin responsiveness, we correlated all insulin-regulated phosphopeptides with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated muscles, resulting in 37 significantly correlated phosphopeptides (r>0.35 or <–0.35, q-value <0.1, Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The insulin response values of 13 phosphopeptides correlated with insulin-stimulated glucose uptake (r>0.35 or <–0.35, q-value <0.1).
source: We found that the insulin response values of 13 phosphopeptides correlated with insulin-stimulated glucose uptake (r>0.35 or <–0.35, q-value <0.1, Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results.

claim: S469 on Pfkfb2 activates glycolysis.
source: These were largely distinct from the 37 phosphopeptides identified in our first analysis, indicating that the two approaches captured complementary information. Several of these phosphopeptides could regulate insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, such as the regulatory site S469 on the enzyme Pfkfb2 which activates glycolysis, a major pathway for glucose consumption (Deprez et al., 1997; Marsin et al., 2000; Ros and Schulze, 2013; Figure 6e), and S177 on Rcsd1, which could affect GLUT4 vesicle transport via actin cytoskeleton remodelling (Stöckli et al., 2011; Figure 6d).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two WGCNA-derived insulin signalling subnetworks correlated with glucose uptake: subnetwork V (r=0.436, p=0.00173) and subnetwork I (r=0.332, p=0.0197).
source: Interestingly, two WGCNA-derived insulin signalling subnetworks correlated with glucose uptake: subnetwork V (r=0.436, p=0.00173) and subnetwork I (r=0.332, p=0.0197, Figure 6f).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Pfkfb3 overexpression increased glycolytic capacity in L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes as measured by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR).
source: As anticipated, Pfkfb3 overexpression increased glycolytic capacity in L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes as measured by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Pfkfb3 overexpression restored insulin-responsive glucose uptake to normal levels in palmitate-treated L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes.
source: Pfkfb3 overexpression also restored insulin-responsive glucose uptake to normal levels in palmitate-treated cells (Figure 6h; Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Genetic background influenced both the phosphoproteomic insulin response of chow-fed mice, as well as how these responses were modified by high-fat, high-sugar feeding.
source: Strikingly, we found that genetic background influenced both the phosphoproteomic insulin response of chow-fed mice, as well as how these responses were modified by high-fat, high-sugar feeding.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Genetic and diet-driven signalling changes did not transmit linearly through the current model of the insulin signalling network.
source: Genetic and diet-driven signalling changes did not transmit linearly through our current model of the insulin signalling network, illustrating that this model remains incomplete.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing complex signalling patterns.

claim: Substrates of kinases such as Akt clustered into distinct groups based on differing insulin responses.
source: Notably, substrates of kinases such as Akt clustered into distinct groups based on differing insulin responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by the clustering analysis of Akt substrates.

claim: It is an oversimplification to model signalling pathways as networks of individual kinases since substrates of the same kinase display independent regulation.
source: Hence, it is an oversimplification to model signalling pathways as networks of individual kinases since substrates of the same kinase display independent regulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed heterogeneity in substrate regulation.

claim: Muscle insulin signalling responses vary across individuals.
source: Muscle insulin signalling responses vary across individuals (Needham et al., 2022; Tonks et al., 2013), and our results suggest that baseline genetic differences and an individual's environment both alter signalling, with the environment's influence depending strongly on genetic background.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and the current study's findings.

claim: Insulin responses in C57Bl6J are not necessarily generalisable to other mouse strains.
source: Our data indicate that insulin responses in C57BL6J – the most commonly studied mouse strain – are not necessarily generalisable, indicated by phosphosites such as S15 on Rnmt that were insulin regulated almost exclusively in C57Bl6J.
evidence: This statement is supported by the observation of strain-specific insulin responses.

claim: Only several dozen insulin-regulated phosphopeptides associated significantly with glucose uptake.
source: It was striking that only several dozen insulin-regulated phosphopeptides associated significantly with glucose uptake.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the correlation analysis.

claim: None of the four primary Akt regulatory sites on Tbc1d4 featured strong positive correlations with glucose uptake.
source: For example, while mutation of the four primary Akt regulatory sites on Tbc1d4 blocks GLUT4 translocation (Sano et al., 2003), none of these phosphosites featured strong positive correlations with glucose uptake in our analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by the correlation analysis and a citation to prior work.

claim: This study focused on male mice and examined only five inbred strains.
source: First, this study focused on male mice and examined only five inbred strains.
evidence: This is a statement of the study design.

claim: The limited number of strains may mean that the association analysis was underpowered to detect some regulators of insulin responsiveness.
source: This limited number of strains may mean that our association analysis was underpowered to detect some regulators of insulin responsiveness.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Mouse insulin sensitivity was affected by interactions between sex and strain.
source: In addition, studies incorporating male and female subjects found that mouse insulin sensitivity was affected by interactions between sex and strain (Parks et al., 2015), and insulin signalling in stem cell-derived myoblasts by interactions between sex and donor metabolic health (Haider et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Insulin signalling in stem cell-derived myoblasts was affected by interactions between sex and donor metabolic health.
source: In addition, studies incorporating male and female subjects found that mouse insulin sensitivity was affected by interactions between sex and strain (Parks et al., 2015), and insulin signalling in stem cell-derived myoblasts by interactions between sex and donor metabolic health (Haider et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Only insulin signalling after 10 min was examined in this study.
source: Second, we only examined insulin signalling after 10 min, since measuring multiple timepoints would have drastically increased the number of animals and samples required.
evidence: This is a statement of the study design.

claim: Protein abundance should not change within a 10 min insulin stimulation.
source: However, since protein abundance should not change within a 10 min insulin stimulation (Fazakerley et al., 2023), the acute insulin responses we observed should only reflect differences in protein phosphorylation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In previous studies of insulin signalling in adipocytes or human skeletal muscle with deep proteomes measured in parallel, there was little global correlation between changes in protein phosphorylation and protein abundance across experimental conditions.
source: Furthermore, in our previous studies of insulin signalling in adipocytes (Fazakerley et al., 2023) or human skeletal muscle (Needham et al., 2022) in which deep proteomes were measured in parallel, we found little global correlation between changes in protein phosphorylation and protein abundance across experimental conditions regardless of insulin stimulation, suggesting the contribution of protein abundance to phosphosite changes across strains and diets was likely minimal.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mice were housed at 23°C on a 12 hr light/dark cycle in cages of 2–5, with free access to food and water.
source: Mice were housed at 23°C on a 12 hr light/dark cycle in cages of 2–5, with free access to food and water.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Mice were randomly allocated to a standard CHOW diet or a high-fat high-sucrose diet at 12–16 weeks of age and sacrificed exactly 6 weeks later.
source: At 12–16 weeks of age mice were randomly allocated to a standard CHOW diet (13% calories from fat, 65% from carbohydrate, 22% from protein; 'Irradiated Rat and Mouse Diet', Specialty Feeds, Glen Forrest, WA, Australia) or a high-fat high-sucrose diet made in house (HFD; 45% calories from fat [40% calories from lard], 35% from carbohydrate [14% calories from starch], and 22% from protein) and sacrificed exactly 6 weeks later.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The EasyPhos workflow and data-independent acquisition (DIA) mass spectrometry were used for phosphoproteomics.
source: Using the EasyPhos workflow and data-independent acquisition (DIA) mass spectrometry (Humphrey et al., 2018; Bekker-Jensen et al., 2020), we quantified 28,809 phosphopeptides across 95 biological samples, corresponding to 23,126 unique high-confidence phosphosites (class I; localisation score >0.75) on 3507 proteins (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods with citations.

claim: Skeletal muscle is the site of greatest post-prandial glucose uptake.
source: We focused on skeletal muscle, as it is the site of greatest post-prandial glucose uptake and the most significant contributor to impaired glucose disposal in type 2 diabetes (DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Skeletal muscle is the most significant contributor to impaired glucose disposal in type 2 diabetes.
source: We focused on skeletal muscle, as it is the site of greatest post-prandial glucose uptake and the most significant contributor to impaired glucose disposal in type 2 diabetes (DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The soleus muscle's largely oxidative fibre composition resembles human muscle tissue more than other murine muscles.
source: Specifically, we chose to examine the soleus muscle, because its largely oxidative fibre composition resembles human muscle tissue more than other murine muscles (Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nos3 S1176 is known to be phosphorylated in response to insulin to promote in vivo glucose uptake by vasodilation.
source: The most significantly correlated phosphopeptide contained T1174 and S1176 on the nitric oxide synthase Nos3. The latter serves as a positive control for our analysis, as this site is known to be phosphorylated in response to insulin to promote in vivo glucose uptake by vasodilation (Roy et al., 1998; Bahadoran et al., 2020; Dimmeler et al., 1999; Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reduced glycolytic flux impairs GLUT4 translocation and insulin signalling.
source: We have previously demonstrated that reduced glycolytic flux impairs GLUT4 translocation and insulin signalling (Trefely et al., 2015), implying that the status of glycolysis is sensed by proteins regulating insulin action.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Glycolytic enzyme abundance was strongly associated with ex vivo insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle from inbred mice.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings that glycolytic enzyme abundance was strongly associated with ex vivo insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle from inbred mice (Nelson et al., 2022), that the insulin resistance-reversing small molecule thiostrepton enhances glycolytic capacity (Masson et al., 2023), and that decreasing glycolytic flux caused insulin resistance in vitro (Trefely et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The insulin resistance-reversing small molecule thiostrepton enhances glycolytic capacity.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings that glycolytic enzyme abundance was strongly associated with ex vivo insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle from inbred mice (Nelson et al., 2022), that the insulin resistance-reversing small molecule thiostrepton enhances glycolytic capacity (Masson et al., 2023), and that decreasing glycolytic flux caused insulin resistance in vitro (Trefely et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Decreasing glycolytic flux caused insulin resistance in vitro.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings that glycolytic enzyme abundance was strongly associated with ex vivo insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle from inbred mice (Nelson et al., 2022), that the insulin resistance-reversing small molecule thiostrepton enhances glycolytic capacity (Masson et al., 2023), and that decreasing glycolytic flux caused insulin resistance in vitro (Trefely et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Pfkfb3 has high basal production rates and lacks an Akt motif at the corresponding phosphosites.
source: By contrast, the paralog Pfkfb3 has high basal production rates and lacks an Akt motif at the corresponding phosphosites (Ros and Schulze, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes display robust insulin regulation of GLUT4 trafficking.
source: To avoid systemic effects of Pfkfb3 overexpression we studied cultured L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes, which display robust insulin regulation of GLUT4 trafficking and develop insulin resistance upon palmitate treatment, mimicking lipotoxicity, a trigger of in vivo insulin resistance (Hoehn et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes develop insulin resistance upon palmitate treatment, mimicking lipotoxicity.
source: To avoid systemic effects of Pfkfb3 overexpression we studied cultured L6-GLUT4-HA myotubes, which display robust insulin regulation of GLUT4 trafficking and develop insulin resistance upon palmitate treatment, mimicking lipotoxicity, a trigger of in vivo insulin resistance (Hoehn et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: C2C12 mouse cell line lack an insulin-responsive vesicular compartment.
source: While L6 cells are of rat origin, they are preferable to the popular C2C12 mouse cell line since the latter lack an insulin-responsive vesicular compartment (Tortorella and Pilch, 2002) and undergo spontaneous contraction, resulting in confounding non-insulin-dependent glucose uptake (Portiér et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: C2C12 cells undergo spontaneous contraction, resulting in confounding non-insulin-dependent glucose uptake.
source: While L6 cells are of rat origin, they are preferable to the popular C2C12 mouse cell line since the latter lack an insulin-responsive vesicular compartment (Tortorella and Pilch, 2002) and undergo spontaneous contraction, resulting in confounding non-insulin-dependent glucose uptake (Portiér et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pfkfb3 overexpression specifically modulated insulin action rather than non-specifically increasing glucose uptake through enhanced glucose consumption.
source: This effect was only observed in cells treated with palmitate and insulin, suggesting it specifically modulated insulin action rather than non-specifically increasing glucose uptake through enhanced glucose consumption (Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This statement is based on the pattern of effects observed in the experimental data.

claim: Immunoblotting of canonical insulin-responsive phosphosites on Akt and its substrates GSK3α/β and PRAS40 revealed minimal effect of palmitate treatment and Pfkfb3 overexpression.
source: However, immunoblotting of canonical insulin-responsive phosphosites on Akt and its substrates GSK3α/β and PRAS40 revealed minimal effect of palmitate treatment and Pfkfb3 overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e–f), hence more detailed phosphoproteomics studies are needed to clarify whether Pfkfb3 overexpression restored insulin action by modulating insulin signalling.
evidence: This statement is based on immunoblotting data.

claim: The five genetically distinct inbred mouse strains studied include C57Bl6J, NOD, BXH9, BXD34, and CAST.
source: To study how protein phosphorylation networks are affected by genetics and environment, we examined insulin signalling in five genetically distinct inbred mouse strains including four lab strains with diverse metabolic phenotypes (C57Bl6J, NOD, BXH9, and BXD34) (Nelson et al., 2022), and the wild-derived CAST strain (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The strains differed in morphometric parameters (body weight, adiposity, lean mass) and metabolic traits (fasting blood glucose, fasting blood insulin, glucose tolerance) both on the CHOW diet and in their response to HFD-feeding.
source: Consistent with their diverse genetics, these strains differed in morphometric parameters (body weight, adiposity, lean mass) and metabolic traits (fasting blood glucose, fasting blood insulin, glucose tolerance) both on the CHOW diet and in their response to HFD-feeding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by the data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Phosphopeptide quantification was minimally affected by the range in soleus mass across strains, with only 12.4% fewer phosphopeptides quantified on average in CAST compared to the C57l6J/NOD.
source: Due to the range in soleus mass across strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d) we altered the protein material used for EasyPhos (C57Bl6J and NOD: 755 µg, BXH9 and BXD34: 511 µg, CAST: 364 µg), though phosphopeptide quantification was minimally affected, with only 12.4% fewer phosphopeptides quantified on average in CAST compared to the C57l6J/NOD (average 13,891.56 vs 15,851.29 Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement is based on comparison of quantification across strains.

claim: Samples from animals of the same strain and diet were highly correlated and generally clustered together.
source: Furthermore, while different strains clustered noticeably by the amount of protein material used, samples from animals of the same strain and diet were still highly correlated and generally clustered together, implying the data are reproducible (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: This statement is based on correlation and clustering analysis.

claim: The study quantified more insulin-regulated phosphopeptides than recent studies of 10 min insulin signalling in patient-derived myoblasts (174 phosphopeptides) and mouse adipose tissue (319 phosphopeptides).
source: This resulted in 441 insulin-regulated phosphopeptides on 232 proteins, which is noticeably more than recent studies of 10 min insulin signalling in patient-derived myoblasts (174 phosphopeptides; Batista et al., 2020) and 242 phosphopeptides (Haider et al., 2021) or mouse adipose tissue (319 phosphopeptides; Fazakerley et al., 2023; Figure 1b and c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement compares the current study's results to prior studies.

claim: Enrichment of Gene Ontology biological processes recapitulated canonical insulin signalling axes including 'insulin receptor signalling pathway', 'phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signalling', 'protein kinase B signalling', and 'TORC1 signalling'.
source: Enrichment of Gene Ontology (GO) biological processes recapitulated canonical insulin signalling axes including 'insulin receptor signalling pathway', 'phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signalling', 'protein kinase B signalling', and 'TORC1 signalling', and multiple pathways related to glucose metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, autophagy, and protein translation, reflecting known targets of insulin action (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This statement is based on GO enrichment analysis.

claim: A small subset of phosphosites were regulated by both insulin in this study and exercise in two separate human phosphoproteomics studies.
source: In addition to insulin, exercise also promotes GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle (Klip et al., 2019). We identified a small subset of phosphosites regulated by insulin in this study that were also regulated by exercise in two separate human phosphoproteomics studies (Needham et al., 2022; Hoffman et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 3d; Supplementary file 2, phosphosites: Eef2 T57 and T59, Mff S129 and S131, Larp1 S498, Tbc1d4 S324, Svil S300, Gys1 S645), providing a starting point for exploring conserved signalling regulators of GLUT4 translocation.
evidence: This statement is based on comparison with prior studies.

claim: Vamp3 S48 may represent a genetically variable control point of GLUT4 trafficking.
source: Vamp3 S48 is predicted to be highly functional (functional score = 0.750) (Ochoa et al., 2020), its phosphorylation correlates with glucose uptake in insulin-stimulated and/or exercised human skeletal muscle (Needham et al., 2022), and Vamp3 overexpression rescues GLUT4 translocation in insulin resistance (Schwenk et al., 2012), suggesting that this site may represent a genetically variable control point of GLUT4 trafficking.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The orchestration of the detrimental signalling axis involving Map2k4, p38, and JNK in HFD-feeding may depend on genetic background.
source: Map2k4 activates p38 and JNK kinases which have been implicated as drivers of HFD-induced insulin resistance (Gehart et al., 2010), and based on the behaviour of S78, the orchestration of this detrimental signalling axis in HFD-feeding may depend on genetic background.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed data.

claim: The strain-affected phosphopeptides reveal a unique fingerprint of insulin signalling within each strain.
source: In all, the strain-affected phosphopeptides reveal a unique fingerprint of insulin signalling within each strain (Figure 2f), highlighting the complex and widespread effects of genetic variation on signalling networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in the heatmap.

claim: The molecular impact of dietary perturbation was strongly modulated by genetic background.
source: Strain×Diet effects were more prevalent than Uniform diet effects (110 vs 10 phosphopeptides, Figure 2g; Supplementary file 1), suggesting that the molecular impact of dietary perturbation was strongly modulated by genetic background.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the prevalence of Strain×Diet effects.

claim: HFD-feeding exerted complex effects on signalling, with the balance between suppressed and enhanced insulin responses varying across strains.
source: HFD-feeding exerted complex effects on signalling, with the balance between suppressed and enhanced insulin responses varying across strains (Figure 2i).
evidence: This statement is based on the analysis of HFD effects across strains.

claim: Insulin-regulated phosphopeptides were largely altered by HFD-feeding in only a single strain.
source: Furthermore, insulin-regulated phosphopeptides were largely altered by HFD-feeding in only a single strain, and when multiple strains were affected, they often changed in opposite directions (Figure 2j–k).
evidence: This statement is based on the analysis of HFD effects.

claim: HFD-feeding displaced each strain in a distinct direction in principal component space.
source: Principal component analysis supported the highly divergent impact of dietary perturbation, as HFD-feeding displaced each strain in a distinct direction in principal component space (Figure 2l).
evidence: This statement is based on PCA analysis.

claim: Strain×Diet and Strain effects were driven by a mixture of changes to insulin-stimulated phosphorylation, unstimulated phosphorylation, or both.
source: Strain×Diet and Strain effects were driven by a mixture of changes to insulin-stimulated phosphorylation, unstimulated phosphorylation, or both, highlighting the complexity of these signalling alterations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f–g).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the types of changes underlying the effects.

claim: Genetic background profoundly modulated the effect of HFD-feeding on insulin signalling.
source: This analysis demonstrates the pervasive role of genetics in shaping signalling networks, as genetic background profoundly modulated the effect of HFD-feeding on insulin signalling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: A network of 160 insulin-regulated phosphosites was curated comprising sites from canonical insulin signalling proteins and substrates of insulin-regulated kinases.
source: To understand the insulin signalling circuitry and functional pathways modulated by genetics and diet, we curated a network of 160 insulin-regulated phosphosites, comprising sites from a knowledge pathway-derived list of canonical insulin signalling proteins (Needham et al., 2022) and substrates of insulin-regulated kinases (Figure 3, see Methods).
evidence: This is a description of the curation process.

claim: No functional pathways were overrepresented within strain or diet-affected phosphosites relative to all insulin-regulated sites.
source: No functional pathways were overrepresented within strain or diet-affected phosphosites relative to all insulin-regulated sites, implying that genetics and environment modulate most or all outcomes of insulin.
evidence: This statement is based on pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Genetics and environment modulate most or all outcomes of insulin.
source: No functional pathways were overrepresented within strain or diet-affected phosphosites relative to all insulin-regulated sites, implying that genetics and environment modulate most or all outcomes of insulin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of pathway enrichment.

claim: All six insulin-regulated phosphosites on Plin1 had Diet effects while only one had a Strain effect.
source: As a notable exception, all six insulin-regulated phosphosites on Plin1 had Diet effects while only one had a Strain effect (Figure 3).
evidence: This statement is based on the analysis of Plin1 phosphosites.

claim: The enrichment of Diet effects on Plin1 may represent a signalling response to increased intramuscular lipids in the HFD condition.
source: Plin1 coats and regulates lipid droplets, hence this enrichment of Diet effects may represent a signalling response to increased intramuscular lipids in the HFD condition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on Plin1's function.

claim: Genetics and environment triggered widespread alterations in insulin signalling impinging on diverse cellular pathways.
source: Overall, genetics and environment triggered widespread alterations in insulin signalling impinging on diverse cellular pathways.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Insulin activated SGK and deactivated GSK3 more in C57Bl6J and NOD than in other strains.
source: For example, insulin activated SGK and deactivated GSK3 more in C57Bl6J and NOD than in other strains (Figure 4b).
evidence: This statement is based on KSEA analysis.

claim: The observed phosphosite signalling changes could be partly due to altered insulin regulation of multiple kinases.
source: These results suggest that the observed phosphosite signalling changes could be partly due to altered insulin regulation of multiple kinases.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the KSEA results.

claim: Similar heterogeneity in Akt substrate insulin responses has previously been observed in skeletal muscle from humans with differing metabolic health.
source: Supporting these findings, similar heterogeneity in Akt substrate insulin responses has previously been observed in skeletal muscle from humans with differing metabolic health (Tonks et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The four groups of Akt substrates may coordinate distinct functional outputs of Akt signalling.
source: Hierarchical clustering revealed four distinct groups of positively correlated Akt substrates (Figure 5a), suggesting these groups may coordinate distinct functional outputs of Akt signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the clustering results.

claim: The subnetworks may be sensitive to distinct cellular information.
source: Examining the subnetwork 'eigenpeptides' – a weighted average of the constituent phosphopeptides (Zhang and Horvath, 2005; Langfelder and Horvath, 2008 )– revealed that the subnetworks captured distinct effects of genetics and diet on insulin signalling (Figure 5e; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a). For example, HFD-feeding attenuated the insulin response of subnetwork I in CAST and C57Bl6J strains (t-test adjusted p=0.0256, 0.0365), while subnetwork II was affected by HFD-feeding only in CAST and NOD (Figure 5e; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, t-test adjusted p=0.00258, 0.0256). This suggests that the subnetworks may be sensitive to distinct cellular information.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects on subnetworks.

claim: Genetic and environmental variation can reveal uncoupling of substrates targeted by the same kinase.
source: Next, we characterised the regulatory and functional nature of these subnetworks. Canonical insulin-regulated kinases such as Akt and mTOR were enriched across multiple subnetworks (Figure 5f), confirming that genetic and environmental variation can reveal uncoupling of substrates targeted by the same kinase (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the subnetwork analysis.

claim: Common localisation may facilitate coregulation of phosphosites.
source: Some subnetworks were enriched in specific cellular compartments (GO), implying that common localisation may facilitate coregulation of phosphosites (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Coregulation may partition functional outcomes of insulin action.
source: Coregulation may partition functional outcomes of insulin action, as certain biological processes were enriched only in select subnetworks (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on pathway enrichment.

claim: Phosphopeptide insulin response dynamics varied across subnetworks.
source: Lastly, we leveraged our previous phosphoproteomic time course of insulin signalling to interrogate subnetwork dynamics (Humphrey et al., 2013) and found that phosphopeptide insulin response dynamics varied across subnetworks (Figure 5i).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis using prior time course data.

claim: Distinct temporal regulation is another feature underlying the substructure of the insulin signalling network.
source: This reveals distinct temporal regulation as another feature underlying the substructure of the insulin signalling network.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal dynamics analysis.

claim: Genetic and environmental diversity illuminated the complex coregulation structure of insulin signalling.
source: Overall, genetic and environmental diversity illuminated the complex coregulation structure of insulin signalling, featuring subnetworks that evade known network circuitry and present unique functional signatures.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the subnetwork analysis findings.

claim: Genetic background and dietary status are key determinants of insulin responsiveness.
source: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake differed by more than twofold across strains (two-way ANOVA strain effect p=4.78 × 10–7) and was almost uniformly decreased by HFD-feeding (two-way ANOVA diet effect p=1.83 × 10–5) (Figure 6a). This highlights that genetic background and dietary status are key determinants of insulin responsiveness.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the glucose uptake measurements.

claim: Of the 34 glucose uptake-associated phosphoproteins identified, 16 were quantified in both this study and a prior proteomics study, and only two additionally correlate with glucose uptake at the total protein level.
source: To assess this, we mined soleus total proteomics data from a recent study of seven CHOW and HFD-fed mouse strains, three of which were in common with this study (C57BL6J, BXH9, BXD34) (Nelson et al., 2022). Of the 34 glucose uptake-associated phosphoproteins we identified, 16 were quantified in both studies and only two additionally correlate with glucose uptake at the total protein level (Ppp6r1 and Ttn, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This statement is based on comparison with prior proteomics data.

claim: Most glucose uptake-phosphosite associations were not driven by protein abundance changes.
source: Hence, it seems likely that most glucose uptake-phosphosite associations were not driven by protein abundance changes, underscoring the utility of phosphoproteomics to provide unique information on top of more classical omics layers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison with proteomics data.

claim: Kinase enrichment scores affected by strain or diet did not correlate with glucose uptake.
source: In addition to individual phosphosites, the status of larger signalling network components could also influence insulin responsiveness. Kinase enrichment scores affected by strain or diet did not correlate with glucose uptake (Supplementary file 4), suggesting insulin action is not dominated by the net activity of specific kinases.
evidence: This statement is based on correlation analysis.

claim: Insulin action is not dominated by the net activity of specific kinases.
source: Kinase enrichment scores affected by strain or diet did not correlate with glucose uptake (Supplementary file 4), suggesting insulin action is not dominated by the net activity of specific kinases.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of correlation.

claim: Subnetwork V could modulate glucose uptake through actin cytoskeleton remodelling, glucose metabolism promotion, and by influencing GLUT4 vesicle trafficking.
source: Subnetwork V could modulate glucose uptake through actin cytoskeleton remodelling via Rscd1 S177, through glucose metabolism promotion via Gys1 S641 (Supplementary file 3), and by influencing GLUT4 vesicle trafficking due to its enrichment at 'cytoplasmic vesicle membranes' (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the composition of subnetwork V.

claim: Subnetwork V was enriched in substrates of GSK3, which has been implicated in insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
source: It was also enriched in substrates of GSK3, which has been implicated in insulin resistance in skeletal muscle (Dokken et al., 2005; Henriksen and Teachey, 2007; Ring et al., 2003) and adipose tissue (Fazakerley et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Subnetwork I may be a central regulatory hub for various outcomes of insulin action including glucose uptake.
source: Subnetwork I, the largest cluster containing 27% of insulin-regulated phosphopeptides, was enriched in multiple kinases and biological processes (Figure 5f and h), suggesting it may be a central regulatory hub for various outcomes of insulin action including glucose uptake.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the composition of subnetwork I.

claim: Compartmentalisation of insulin-responsive phosphosites into subnetworks may enable independent control of insulin's functional outputs.
source: Overall, compartmentalisation of insulin-responsive phosphosites into subnetworks may enable independent control of insulin's functional outputs, since only two subnetworks correlated with insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the subnetwork analysis.

claim: Phosphorylation of Pfkfb2 S469 leads to increased production of F2,6BP, a potent glycolytic agonist.
source: S469 on Pfkfb2 correlated highly with glucose uptake follow insulin stimulation (Figure 6e). Phosphorylation of this site leads to increased production of F2,6BP, a potent glycolytic agonist, suggesting that activating glycolysis may play a key role in muscle insulin responsiveness.
evidence: This statement is based on known biochemistry of Pfkfb2.

claim: Activating glycolysis may play a key role in muscle insulin responsiveness.
source: Phosphorylation of this site leads to increased production of F2,6BP, a potent glycolytic agonist, suggesting that activating glycolysis may play a key role in muscle insulin responsiveness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the correlation and biochemistry.

claim: Pfkfb2 requires phosphorylation by Akt to produce F2,6BP substantially.
source: Since Pfkfb2 requires phosphorylation by Akt to produce F2,6BP substantially, increasing F2,6BP production via Pfkfb2 would require enhanced activating site phosphorylation, which is difficult to achieve in a targeted fashion, or phosphomimetic mutation of activating sites to aspartate/glutamate, which often does not recapitulate the molecular effects of serine/threonine phosphorylation (Dephoure et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is based on known biochemistry and a citation.

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation of activating sites to aspartate/glutamate often does not recapitulate the molecular effects of serine/threonine phosphorylation.
source: Since Pfkfb2 requires phosphorylation by Akt to produce F2,6BP substantially, increasing F2,6BP production via Pfkfb2 would require enhanced activating site phosphorylation, which is difficult to achieve in a targeted fashion, or phosphomimetic mutation of activating sites to aspartate/glutamate, which often does not recapitulate the molecular effects of serine/threonine phosphorylation (Dephoure et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpressing Pfkfb3 would robustly increase F2,6BP production and enhance glycolysis regardless of insulin stimulation and Akt signalling.
source: We therefore rationalised that overexpressing Pfkfb3 would robustly increase F2,6BP production and enhance glycolysis regardless of insulin stimulation and Akt signalling (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is a rationale based on the properties of Pfkfb3.

claim: The catalogue of glucose uptake-correlated phosphosites will provide a rich starting point for future investigations into mechanisms of insulin action and resistance.
source: We anticipate that our catalogue of glucose uptake-correlated phosphosites will provide a rich starting point for future investigations into mechanisms of insulin action and resistance.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the utility of the data.

claim: Validation studies in L6 myotubes confirmed the major role of accelerated glycolysis as a key regulator of insulin responsiveness.
source: Finally, validation studies in L6 myotubes confirmed the major role of accelerated glycolysis as a key regulator of insulin responsiveness.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the validation experiments.

claim: Substrates of the same kinase can be differentially regulated by genetic and environmental variation.
source: KSEA predicted changes in overall kinase activity, but we questioned if substrates of the same kinase could be differentially regulated by genetic and environmental variation.
evidence: This is a question that was addressed by the analysis.

claim: Associating changes in protein phosphorylation across the gene-by-environment landscape with phenotypic change would dissect mechanistic targets with greater fidelity.
source: A major challenge in phosphoproteomics studies is pinpointing important regulatory events among the many responding to a stimulus. We reasoned that associating changes in protein phosphorylation across the gene-by-environment landscape with phenotypic change – in this case insulin-stimulated glucose uptake – would dissect mechanistic targets with greater fidelity.
evidence: This is a rationale for the approach taken.

claim: The work represents the first global portrait of insulin signalling network plasticity in response to genetic and environmental variation.
source: Our work represents the first global portrait of insulin signalling network plasticity in response to genetic and environmental variation, which will serve as an important resource in future studies of insulin action and resistance.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the work.
